newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HSBC seen unlikely to buy big Austrialian bank.
newsitem.headline: HSBC seen unlikely to buy big Austrialian bank.

text.p: Banking giant HSBC Holdings Plc is unlikely to bid for Australia New Zealand Banking Group Ltd in the near future because the risk-reward relationship does not support such a deal, Hong Kong-based banking analysts said on Monday.

Analysts believe ANZ would be too costly and high risk, not the type of expansion move characteristic of HSBC, despite the recent resurrection of rumours that HSBC's Hongkong Bank of Australia is about to bid for it.
"It is a large acquisition. The size adds to the risk complexity," said a banking analyst with a large U.S. broker.
"HSBC has the resources (to acquire ANZ) but it is not featured in our recommendation (on HSBC stock)," he added.
This is not the first time acquisition rumours have bubbled.

"For years there have been rumours that Hongkong Bank was interested in acquiring WestPac, but recently the target (in the rumours) has changed to ANZ," said Carmel Welso, regional banking analyst at ING Barings in Hong Kong.
ANZ's share price has risen sharply in the past four months on rumours it was a takeover target by local and foreign banks. HSBC has been mentioned as a possible bidder.
ANZ opened at A$7.164 on Monday, then rose to A$7.28, a new intraday high before dropping back to trade at A$7.23.
"Given that ANZ is the only one of the four major Australian banking groups with overseas operations, one of the other three would probably be a better choice," Welso said.
The other three are Westpac Banking Corp, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, and National Australia Bank Ltd.
"ANZ is the only one of the four that has not undergone restructuring, so there could be considerable corporate fat to cut," Welso added.
Analysts have suggested that two-times book value is a good pricing benchmark.

As of end-September 1995, ANZ had shareholders' funds of A$5.70 billion, thus suggesting a potential value for the entire banking group of more than A$13 billion, assuming growth in earnings and assets in 1996 and 1997.
In contrast, HongKong Bank of Australia had total net assets of A$3.57 billion as of the end of 1995.
Another Hong Kong-based analyst suggested that ANZ is indeed a takeover target but by a local bank, not by HSBC. "An in-market acquisition would make more sense," the analyst said.
HSBC spokesman Robert Sherbin declined to comment on the rumours. "We are aware that a rumour is circulating in the market. We do not comment on rumours," he said.

Hongkong Bank won an Australian banking license in 1986 along with several other foreign and local banks in that nation's mid-1980's wave of reform and deregulation. However, those newly licensed banks saw more down years than up.
"It has been a highly competitive environment," Sherbin said.

In 1995, HSBC's wholly-owned Australian subsidiary reported attributable profits of A$13 million, a seven percent increase over the year earlier. According to Welso, the bank was consistently loss-making until 1993.
Hongkong Bank of Australia has thirteen branches located mainly in the east in Sydney and Melbourne near Asian Austrialian communities, Sherbin said.
"Our retail banking market niche in Australia is the Asian Australian community, although not solely," he said.
ANZ, on the other hand, is one of Australia's four largest banking groups. In financial year 1995 (ended September 30), the bank reported earnings of A$1.05 billion.
